newsitem.title: FRANCE: French stocks close easier after new high.
newsitem.headline: French stocks close easier after new high.

text.p: French shares closed easier on Tuesday in line with Wall Street but remained above the 2,300 level after having pushed the CAC-40 index to a fresh year high at 2,315.25.

Dealers said investors were cautious about a series of important U.S. statistics due on Thursday and Friday and noted Tuesday's trading had been in a very tight range of between 2,294.93 and 2,315.25.
Wall Street's slide was prompted by falls in bond prices.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index closed down 4.98 points or 0.22 percent at 2,301.69 while the CAC-40 futures contract was down at 2,304 from 2,313 on Monday's close.
Volume was 5.13 billion francs, of which 3.19 billion in CAC-40 shares.

Via Banque was biggest riser of the day, adding 8.43 percent to 180 francs on takeover speculation after insurer AGF sold Banque du Phenix to ABN Amro of the Netherlands. "This deal is rekindling interest in small banks," a broker said.

The biggest faller of the day was BIS which requoted after having been suspended on the morning of December 30 following the death of its founder and chairman Laurent Negro. On Monday, Dutch Vendex International agreed to buy a 60 percent stake at 490 francs per share from Laurent's family.

BIS fell 7.67 percent to close at 492.10 francs. Analysts said that while they judged the 490 franc price low, minority holders did probably not stand much chance of prising a higher price from the Netherlands' retailing and services group.

AXA raded in heavy volume, adding five francs to 338.50 in a volume of 1.17 million shares. Traders said that AXA's weight in the CAC-40 index would be increased next week after the outcome of its share offer bid on UAP and some index tracking funds were buying the share in anticipation.

SGS-Thomson added 0.59 percent to 377.20 francs. Dataquest said that the 1996 semiconductor sales were down seven percent to $141 billion, but this was mainly due a fall in sales of DRAM's. SGS-Thomson and Intel -- which both do not make DRAMs -- were alone among the top nine chip producers to record a revenue gain in 1996, Dataquest said.
